Question five. What is multi-head attention, and why use it? Give each head its own smaller query, key and value, run attention in each, in parallel, and concatenate the results. One head can track syntax, another which noun a pronoun means. And eight heads of sixty-four cost the same multiply-adds as one head of five hundred and twelve. Now the whole model.

Question six. Describe the transformer architecture. A stack of blocks: multi-head self-attention, then a feed-forward network at each position, each wrapped in a residual connection and layer norm. Attention ignores order, so positional encodings add it. Encoder-only models like bert attend both ways, for understanding. Decoder-only models like GPT mask the future, for generation. Encoder-decoder models like T5 turn one sequence into another.

Question seven. Why did transformers replace RNNs for most NLP? An RNN squeezes everything through one hidden state, one step at a time: slow to train, and forgetful over distance. A transformer links any two tokens directly and, in training, processes every position at once, which is what a GPU is built for. The trade-off is attention's own cost.

Question eight. Why is attention's cost a scaling bottleneck for long documents? Every token is compared with every other. A thousand tokens make a million pairs; two thousand, four million. Double the context, and attention costs about four times as much. The rest of a layer only grows linearly, though. For a model four thousand and ninety-six wide, with the usual feed-forward four times that, attention's arithmetic outweighs the rest only past about twenty-five thousand tokens. Past that, teams reach for sparse, sliding-window or linear attention, or retrieve the passages that matter instead of pasting in everything.
